wine.name: Kéknyelű
wine.grapes: Kéknyelű, the blue stalked native white of the Badacsony hills, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: Kéknyelű on the basalt of Badacsony hill above the lake, and part of the last old plot of the grape at Nemesgulács, which the founder bought when the variety was saved, by Magyar Bor's account.
wine.making: The house's own cellar notes could not be read, so no vessel is claimed. Magyar Bor says Kéknyelű is mostly made dry and often given long time in bottle, and that barrel ageing suits it too; the grape flowers as a female, so a pollinating variety grows beside it and is picked and made apart.
wine.glass: Lean and taut: green apple, lime peel and bitter almond over a smoky, stony, saline edge from the basalt, with high, firm acidity and a long, narrow finish that opens slowly with air and age.
wine.ageing: Closed and austere in its first years; its high acidity, the trait that gives the grape its name for long life, lets a good bottle keep and open for many years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Blue stalk: the grape is named for the faint blue tint of its leaf stalks.
The protected wine district around the basalt hill on the northern shore of Lake Balaton.

records.table: After 1990 the founder of Szeremley, at Badacsonytomaj, helped save Kéknyelű, the blue stalked native white of the Balaton hills. The estate's Kéknyelű is lean, smoky and high in acid and slow to open, so it wants a cool glass and some air.
records.story: Huba Szeremley (1940 to 2021) was born in Budapest and left Hungary in 1967, building a fortune abroad. He came back after the change of regime and in the 1990s pieced together a large holding of vineyard land on the Badacsony hills. Kéknyelű, the hills' own white grape, had shrunk after phylloxera and almost vanished in the socialist years, when, by a local account, even the variety collection was cleared and only a few thousand vines were saved; the last old plot was a small vineyard of the Badacsony co-operative at Nemesgulács. With other growers he set about saving it: cuttings were taken from that plot, which he bought in part, and the grape was planted again. It is a hard vine to grow, with only female flowers, so a pollinating variety must stand beside it, and it sets small, uneven bunches. By the time he died in May 2021, Kéknyelű was planted again across the district, and his part in the revival is told by the national wine body and by the wine press alike. In 2016 his house and two of his vineyards went to auction, but the estate kept his name. The story of the grape's return begins with Szeremley's Kéknyelű.

The region record and the plan say the house brought Kéknyelű back; Magyar Bor names two other growers beside him (one of them possibly living, so not named), so the record says he helped save it with others.
World of Fine Wine calls him an engineer whose fortune came from Africa; Infostart says he studied theology and medicine; the record says only that he built a fortune abroad.
Infostart calls him the founder of the Pannon Bormíves Céh; no second source confirms it, so it is left out.

The making field gives Magyar Bor's account of the grape, not this house's cellar, which no source read describes; the glass rests on the grape's high acidity in Jancis Robinson's note and the plan's lean, slow to open profile.
A family member named in tasting notes is living and not named; the auction of much of the estate (HVG, February 2016; Pénzcentrum, 2021) is told as history.

wine.name: Szürkebarát
wine.grapes: Szürkebarát, the Hungarian name for Pinot Gris, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the basalt witness hills of the lake, whose main parcels lie on Badacsony and Csobánc, by the house's account; the house does not name the parcels of this bottling.
wine.making: Made dry in the house's cellar at Badacsony, by its own account with a drop of residual sugar left in to round the wine; its notes give no vessel or ageing, so none is claimed here.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, acacia blossom and a hint of white pepper, full and round in the mouth, softened by the touch of sweetness the house leaves; richer than a Pinot Grigio and closer to Alsace in weight, as Badacsony's Szürkebarát runs.
wine.ageing: Drink it young, within a few years of the vintage, while its pear and blossom are fresh; the house gives no ageing advice of its own.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

records.table: A small press house above the lake, given as a wedding present in 1978, grew into Laposa, a Badacsony family estate. In its Szürkebarát, Pinot Gris takes Badacsony's fuller way: pear and acacia blossom with a touch of sweetness, closer to Alsace than to Pinot Grigio.
records.story: The house tells its story from 1978, when two families met in marriage at the Hableány, the old lakeside hotel of Badacsony opened in 1883: the Laposas of Budapest, who were coopers, and the Barabás family of Badacsony, who grew vines. The young couple were given a small press house in the Balaton Uplands as a wedding present, and the family spent more and more time there. Magyar Bor's register gives 1990 as the founding of the estate; from the early 1990s it grew, choosing land across the Badacsony wine district, with its main parcels on Badacsony itself and on Csobánc, and by the house's own account its first vines were planted in 1992 and the Istenmeredekje vineyard in 1994. In 1997 the first labelled, bottled Laposa wines appeared, by the house's account, and in 2019 the Hableány, where the founders had married, was restored as the estate's centre. Laposa works almost wholly in white wine and in the district's own grapes: Olaszrizling, Rajnai Rizling, Kéknyelű, Furmint and Szürkebarát, which Magyar Bor counts with Olaszrizling and Kéknyelű among Badacsony's three traditional leading varieties. Its Szürkebarát shows what that historic grape gives on basalt by the lake: a fuller, rounder Pinot Gris than the Italian style.

wine.name: Rajnai Rizling
wine.grapes: Rajnai Rizling, Rhine Riesling, alone: the estate grows no other grape.
wine.sites: South facing vineyards in the core of Badacsony hill, among them, by the house's account, parcels of the former Esterházy and Ranolder estates; the Kezdet vineyard, very stony and rich in basalt, gives Rare Peak wines.
wine.making: Yields are kept low and the harvest is drawn late into the season, by the house's account. Press fractions and parcels are fermented apart in steel tanks and the wines are blended from tank; the single vineyard wines are fermented and matured in steel, and fermentation is at times stopped with a little sugar left.
wine.glass: Lime, green apple and white peach over a smoky, stony note of the basalt, with Riesling's high, firm acidity and, in some cuvées, a trace of sweetness to balance it.
wine.ageing: Approachable young; Riesling's high acidity lets the stonier single vineyard wines keep longer, for a span the house does not set.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle; a white wine glass with a narrow rim.

label.means: Rhine Riesling, the true Riesling, under its Hungarian name.

records.table: One grape alone grows at Villa Sandahl, the Badacsony estate founded by Swedes in 2004: Rajnai Rizling, the true Riesling. Fermented apart by parcel in steel, its wines set lime and green apple against the smoky stone of the basalt hill.
records.story: Villa Sandahl began in 2004, when two Swedish founders of the Sandahl family and their families bought vineyards on Badacsony hill. By their own account they chose Hungary because vineyards of real quality could then be bought by private wine lovers, and the slopes they found were south facing, at the core of the hill, among them, as the house tells it, land of the former Esterházy and Ranolder estates. Those slopes proved a little too warm for early ripening grapes, so the founders settled on Rajnai Rizling, Rhine Riesling, which ripens late and keeps its acidity, and head grafted or replanted their vines to it. The estate grows nothing else, and every wine is a Riesling, given its own name by vintage, parcel or pressing, and the house keeps yields low and picks late. In the cellar the press fractions and the parcels are fermented apart in steel tanks and the wines are blended from tank, the stoniest, from the basalt of the Kezdet vineyard, kept apart under the Rare Peak name, the house's premium grade. In May 2016 the estate opened a guesthouse, the Sandahl Rezidencia, and in 2024 it marked its twentieth year. Here is the plain case for Riesling on Badacsony basalt, in a district better known for Olaszrizling.

wine.name: Csobáncz Olaszrizling
wine.grapes: Olaszrizling, Welschriesling, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards at the foot of Csobánc, a volcanic witness hill north of the lake, on soils weathered from its basalt.
wine.making: By the house's own account the must settles naturally for some hours, then ferments spontaneously with its own yeasts in steel tanks or in large Stockinger oak casks, and the wine is given a long time on its lees before it is racked.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, green apple and almond, with ripe peach and a salty edge on the finish; dry and firm, with the bitter almond close that marks Olaszrizling and a tight, stony line.
wine.ageing: Good young and fresh; its acidity carries it for several years, though the house gives no figure.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

records.table: Villa Tolnay takes its name from the actress who once stayed in its house on Csobánc, a volcanic hill behind Badacsony. Its Csobáncz Olaszrizling is dry, firm and salty, lemon and almond from basalt soil, wild fermented and long on its lees.
records.story: Local accounts tie the house at the foot of Csobánc to Klári Tolnay (1914 to 1998), an actress of the Hungarian stage and screen: the vineyard was once her first husband's, and she spent part of the Second World War there. In 2004 a Swiss wine lover bought her former villa, drawn by the view from the hill, and founded a winery there, keeping her name for it. The estate grew steadily from that start, almost all of it on Csobánc, one of the volcanic witness hills that rise from the Tapolca basin north of the lake, where the vines grow on soils weathered from basalt. The house grows both Rieslings, Rajnai Rizling and Olaszrizling, with Zöldveltelini, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Furmint, and makes its wines by a rule of its own: a short natural settling of the must, a spontaneous ferment in steel or in large Austrian casks and a long time on the yeast. Its first sparkling wine, an Extra Brut Furmint made in bottle, came with the 2020 vintage. The Csobáncz Olaszrizling, labelled under the wider Balatoni name with the hill's old spelling, is the house's word on the Balaton's everyday grape: the same Olaszrizling as Csopak's, given the structure of a volcanic hill.

wine.name: Lőczedombi Olaszrizling
wine.grapes: Olaszrizling, Welschriesling, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: Lőczedomb, a single vineyard on the slopes of Lőcze hill above Csopak, on thick red Permian sandstone, the soil that marks the district east of Csopak.
wine.making: For the 2024 vintage, by Magyar Bor's notes, half was fermented spontaneously and aged for four months in 225 litre French barrels and half fermented and aged in steel tanks before the two were brought together; the share may move with the vintage.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon peel and bitter almond, the almond close of Olaszrizling, with a light toast from the barrel half and a salty, fine boned line from the red sandstone.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of the vintage, though its acidity lets it keep several more; the house names no span.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

records.table: On the old wine estate of a nineteenth century bishop of Veszprém, at Csopak, Jásdi makes its Lőczedombi Olaszrizling from red Permian sandstone on Lőcze hill, half in French barrels and half in steel: green apple, almond and a salty line.
records.story: János Ranolder (1806 to 1875), Bishop of Veszprém from 1850, began buying land at Csopak in 1853 and built a wine estate there in stages, one that helped put the village on the wine map; he died at Csopak. In 1998 the Jásdi family took on the bishop's old estate, and their cellar stands in its old building. From 2002 they made an Olaszrizling and Furmint cuvée, Ranolder White, named for the bishop, since that pairing was a Csopak tradition, by the house's account. In 2012 a group of Csopak producers, Jásdi among them, created the Csopak Codex, a mark for Olaszrizling of the village, with at most a little Furmint, chosen each year by blind tasting. Lőczedomb lies on Lőcze hill above the village, on the thick red Permian sandstone that marks the land east of Csopak, a soil quite unlike the basalt of Badacsony. Csopak lies in the Balatonfüred-Csopak district, not in Badacsony, and Jásdi stands here as the Balaton's sandstone answer to the basalt hills: the same grape, a different stone.

report: The plan's merge read is borne out: Csopak lies in the Balatonfüred-Csopak district, not Badacsony, and the record says so plainly. A swap is proposed for the checker: a house of the Badacsony district itself, Istvándy of Káptalantóti (its own Kéknyelű, a Kéknyelű sparkling wine first shown in 2012, by its own account) or the Borbély estate, both named by Magyar Bor among Badacsony's Kéknyelű makers; either would need its own research, and Istvándy would double Szeremley's grape.
The bishop's dates rest on Catholic Hierarchy (born 16 May 1806, died 12 September 1875 at Csopak, Bishop of Veszprém from 1850) and the purchases from 1853 on the Csopak village heritage study.
The family's start in 1998 rests on Magyar Bor's register and a Balaton tourism profile; one writer's profile says the estate was bought in 2002, perhaps a later stage, and is not followed.

The 2013 Lőczedombi as a Codex wine rests on one regional report (We Love Balaton, 2014) and is told without hedge only because the Codex itself is on Magyar Bor's district page; the checker should test it.
The plan's old vines are left out for want of a source; the making is the 2024 vintage's as Magyar Bor's notes give it, and said so.
Whether the label carries the Balatonfüred-Csopak name or Csopaki could not be confirmed; the appellation field gives the district.
The living founder and family are not named.

changed: story: was that the estate declined for half a century and was close to a ruin by the 1990s, found in no source of this check (a regional source has the bishop's estate selling to Vienna in the 1880s); now only that the family took on the old estate in 1998, its cellar in the old building.

story, trap and the story question: the Codex was a mark for Olaszrizling alone from twenty six protected vineyards with the Lőczedombi of 2013 chosen; now a mark for the village's Olaszrizling with at most a little Furmint (Magyar Bor gives a cap of 15 per cent), chosen yearly by blind tasting, with Jásdi among its producers; the count of vineyards and the 2013 choice were found in no source of this check.
story and others: Ranolder White now made since 2002 (Wine Folly's guide) and its pairing hedged as the house's account (its BOR 2025 sheet).
open: Magyar Bor says Csopak producers brought in a Csopak PDO of their own in 2017; whether the Lőczedombi label carries Csopak rather than Balatonfüred-Csopak was not settled, so the appellation keeps the district both BOR listings give.
Jásdi stands outside the Badacsony district; the swap is agreed in principle and left to the integrator (see the review file).
